title: Memory Model & Storage Classes
relevance: SDE interviews probe whether candidates can reason about where C data lives, how long it lives, and bugs from mixing scope, lifetime, and linkage.

phases.goal: Establish the process address-space layout and the four storage durations the C standard defines.

must_hit.point: A process gets an isolated virtual address space; every byte in RAM has a unique numeric address.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions virtual memory as an OS illusion of a private contiguous address space from zero to the architectural max.

must_hit.point: Loaded C programs typically use five segments: Text (read-only code), Initialized Data, BSS (zeroed globals/statics), Heap, and Stack.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all five regions and maps globals with explicit init to Data, zero/uninit globals to BSS, locals to stack, malloc to heap.

must_hit.point: Heap typically grows upward toward higher addresses; stack typically starts high and grows downward toward the heap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States opposite growth directions so the two pools share the unused middle of the address space.

must_hit.point: C defines four storage durations: automatic, static, allocated, and thread (_Thread_local, C11).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the four durations and notes automatic for locals, static for program lifetime, allocated via malloc/free, thread for a thread's life.

must_hit.point: String literals live in read-only memory (typically with/near Text), not on stack or heap; modifying them is Undefined Behavior.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says "Hello"-style literals are read-only and that writing through a char* to one is UB (often a segfault).

probes: Walk through where public_count, pending_flags, local_temp, and a malloc'd array land in the process address space.
Why do stack and heap grow toward each other instead of both growing upward from the bottom?

hints.1: Think of the process like an office building with separate regions for code, globals, locals, and dynamic boxes.
hints.2: OS load partitions virtual memory into Text, Data, BSS, Heap, and Stack—heap up from BSS, stack down from high addresses.
hints.3: Initialized non-zero globals → Data; zero/uninit globals → BSS (sized on disk, zeroed at start); locals → stack; malloc → heap; code/literals → read-only Text area.

phases.goal: Explain how storage-class specifiers, the dual meaning of static, linkage/ODR, and init rules actually control objects.

must_hit.point: File-scope static gives internal linkage (private to the translation unit); block-scope static keeps local scope but switches lifetime from automatic to static.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts static int outside a function (hidden to other .c files) with static inside a function (initialized once, retains value across calls).

must_hit.point: Linkage is none (locals), internal (file-scope static), or external (default for globals/functions across the whole program).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines the three linkage kinds and ties internal linkage to file-scope static.

must_hit.point: You may declare a global many times but must define it exactly once: extern in a header, definition without extern in one .c file.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes declaration vs definition and the header-extern + single-.c-definition pattern for sharing a global.

must_hit.point: Scope answers where a name is visible in source; lifetime answers when the object's memory exists at runtime—they are independent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States a block-scope static can have local name visibility but program-long memory.

must_hit.point: Uninitialized static/thread objects are zeroed (NULL for pointers); uninitialized automatic and allocated objects have indeterminate values.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites the duration-based default init rules and warns that reading uninit locals is garbage/UB-adjacent.

probes: What two jobs does static perform depending on whether it is at file scope or inside a function?
How do you share one global across multiple .c files without violating the one-definition rule?

hints.1: static is overloaded—ask where the keyword appears before deciding what it means.
hints.2: Outside functions: linkage (internal). Inside functions: lifetime (static). Sharing globals needs extern declarations plus one definition.
hints.3: File-scope static = internal linkage; block-scope static = local scope + static duration, init once before main; put extern in .h and define once in one .c.

phases.goal: Compare stack versus heap as engineering choices for where data lives.

must_hit.point: Stack allocation is extremely fast (adjust the stack pointer); heap allocation via malloc is slower due to bookkeeping and possible OS page requests.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts moving a register vs calling malloc with internal accounting.

must_hit.point: Stack lifetime is bound to the function/block and cleaned up automatically; heap lifetime is manual until free.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says stack frames pop on return; heap persists until free or leaks if forgotten.

must_hit.point: Stack is very small (often limited to 1MB to 8MB by the OS); heap is massive, limited by RAM/virtual memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites the small OS stack cap versus heap sized by available system memory.

must_hit.point: Stack overflow (huge locals/deep recursion) crashes immediately; heap failure modes include leaks and use-after-free UB.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names stack overflow vs leak / access-after-free as the characteristic failures.

probes: When would you put a large buffer on the heap instead of as a local array, and what costs does that buy you?

hints.1: Compare speed, who frees the memory, and how big each region is allowed to be.
hints.2: Stack: fast, auto, tiny, overflow. Heap: slower, manual, large, leak/UAF.
hints.3: Prefer stack for small short-lived locals; use heap when size/lifetime must outlive the frame or exceed the OS stack limit (often 1MB to 8MB).

phases.goal: Apply layout, static persistence, and lifetime rules to real bug patterns and classification.

must_hit.point: Returning a pointer to a local is a critical bug: the stack frame is invalidated on return, leaving a dangling pointer and UB on use.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains the frame is popped, the pointer is dangling, and the next call may overwrite that memory.

must_hit.point: A block-scope static retains value across calls while a same-function automatic reinitializes every call.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Traces generate_id-style behavior: next_id persists and increments; temp resets to 0 each call.

must_hit.point: malloc'd memory has no name/scope of its own—only allocated duration and access via pointers; no linkage.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Classifies the object behind epsilon as nameless, allocated duration, no linkage.

must_hit.point: Block-scope statics are shared across threads calling the same function, so unprotected use races.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Notes multithreaded callers share one static cell and need a mutex if mutated.

probes: Why is returning a pointer to a local variable a critical bug?
Classify alpha, beta, gamma, delta, and the malloc'd object by scope, storage duration, and linkage.

hints.1: Ask what happens to the stack frame the moment the function returns.
hints.2: Locals die with the frame; block-scope static lives in Data/BSS for the whole run; heap objects live until free and have no identifier of their own.
hints.3: Returned &local is dangling UB; static local persists across calls; file globals differ by external vs internal linkage; malloc object = allocated duration, no scope/linkage.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Stack is extremely fast (stack-pointer bump), automatically freed with the frame, but tiny (often 1MB to 8MB) and fails via stack overflow. Heap is slower (malloc bookkeeping / OS pages), manually lifetime-managed with free, essentially limited by RAM/virtual memory, and fails via leaks or use-after-free UB.

gotchas.trap: Assuming string literals live on the stack or heap and can be written through a char*.
gotchas.correction: Literals are in read-only memory (typically with/near Text); modifying them is Undefined Behavior and usually segfaults.

gotchas.trap: Thinking static inside a function means the variable is constant/unchangeable.
gotchas.correction: It means persistent lifetime across calls; the value can still be modified freely.

gotchas.trap: Using a block-scope static as per-call private state in multithreaded code.
gotchas.correction: That static is shared by all threads calling the function; protect mutations with a mutex or avoid the pattern.
Automatic (and allocated) objects without initializers hold indeterminate values; reading may be UB if a trap representation exists—always initialize locals.

gotchas.trap: Returning a pointer to a local variable.
gotchas.correction: The stack frame is popped on return; the pointer dangles and later use is Undefined Behavior.
